definition: Hail damage roof repair restores the roof covering at each hail impact point — bruised and fractured shingles, granule loss, and dented metal flashing — and documents the damage for an insurance claim. It classifies functional damage that exposes the asphalt mat against cosmetic surface marking.

signs: Circular bruises and soft spots felt when a shingle is pressed indicate mat fracture beneath intact granules — the primary functional hail-damage sign — per IBHS hail-assessment guidance.

Random-pattern granule loss exposing the black asphalt mat indicates hail scuffed the protective granule layer, the onset of lost service life on impacted shingles — per the American Meteorological Society.
Cracked or split shingle edges and corners indicate angled hail impact on aged, brittle asphalt — per IBHS hail-assessment guidance.

Dented metal gutters, downspouts, vent caps, and flashing indicate hailstones large enough to damage the roof field, because metal denting corroborates the hail size that struck the shingles — per IBHS hail-assessment guidance.
Dents on air-conditioning condenser fins, vehicles, and outdoor equipment indicate hail of damaging size, an industry corroborating indicator for a roof inspection — per IBHS guidance.
Neighboring roofs filing hail claims after the same storm indicate a hail swath crossed the area, because hail damage from one storm concentrates within a defined path — per IBHS hail research.
selectionCriteria: Active New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration — required of every NJ home-improvement contractor under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136; verify the 13VH registration number, which must appear on the contract and in advertising under N.J.S.A. 56:8-144. This is a REGISTRATION, not a license — New Jersey issues no roofing license.

Commercial general liability insurance of at least $500,000 per occurrence (N.J.S.A. 56:8-142), verified by a Certificate of Insurance issued directly by the carrier — not by the contractor's own letterhead.
A written contract for any home-improvement work over $500, signed by both parties, with start/completion dates and the total price (N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2).
A detailed, itemized written estimate that separates labor, materials, product line/color, and the repair-versus-replacement scope so it can be matched against the insurance settlement.
Local references and an established local presence in Essex County — guards against out-of-area storm-chaser contractors who appear after a hail swath and leave before warranty issues surface.

A thorough, documented assessment: a test-square method (a 10-by-10-foot square = one roofing square of 100 sq ft on each slope), per-square impact counts, close-up photographs with measurement references, and a roof diagram — the documentation rigor insurers and independent engineers recognize (IBHS hail-assessment guidance; Insurance Information Institute).

No manufacturer-certification or third-party-inspector-certification self-claim should be required of a competent contractor — well-documented, independent, verifiable assessment plus registered NJ HIC status and insurance is what supports the claim.

technicalFacts.fact: NOAA sets the severe-hail warning threshold at 0.75 inch diameter, but roof damage begins higher: about 1.0 inch on aged 3-tab shingles, about 1.25 inch on most common shingles, with 2.0-inch hail damaging all tested roofing.
technicalFacts.source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA); American Meteorological Society

technicalFacts.fact: Hail damage tracks kinetic energy — hail size combined with wind speed — so a 0.75-inch stone in high wind outdamages a 1.0-inch stone in calm air.
technicalFacts.source: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety (IBHS)

technicalFacts.fact: Hail assessment classifies each impact as functional damage (exposes the asphalt mat and shortens service life) or cosmetic damage (marks the surface without compromising waterproofing); most homeowners policies cover functional hail damage while some exclude cosmetic-only damage.
technicalFacts.source: IBHS hail-assessment guidance; Insurance Information Institute (III)

technicalFacts.fact: Wind and hail rank as the largest homeowners-insurance claim type at 2.8% of insured homes per year (1 in 36), with an average claim of $14,747.

Repair-or-replacement scope follows impact density: scattered impacts on a newer roof allow individual shingle replacement, while a dense impact pattern across the roof favors full replacement priced per square.

UL 2218 Class 4 impact-resistant shingles are the most resistant of the 4 UL 2218 impact classes; IBHS and the Federal Alliance for Safe Homes (FLASH) recommend Class 3 or 4 shingles in hail-exposed areas.
technicalFacts.source: UL 2218; IBHS; Federal Alliance for Safe Homes

technicalFacts.fact: New Jersey records roughly 25–30 thunderstorms per year and sits outside the high-frequency hail region of the Plains, so an Essex County hail event concentrates damage on aged asphalt shingles that have lost impact resilience.

Repair or replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance — no construction permit, inspection, or notice to the construction official required.
On a commercial building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area within a 12-month period requires a permit.

Low-slope membrane life expectancies to document at a commercial hail assessment: EPDM 15–25 years, TPO 7–20 years, modified bitumen ~20 years; hail strikes a low-slope membrane at a more direct angle than a sloped residential roof.

A roof should be inspected after any major storm, including a hailstorm, in addition to the twice-per-year spring and fall inspections; prompt inspection documents impacts before later weather alters the evidence, supporting attribution to a specific storm for an insurance claim.
technicalFacts.source: NRCA (inspection cadence); Insurance Information Institute (claim-documentation rationale)

sources: Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety (IBHS)

defabToKill.issue: HAAG Engineering certification framed as 'the gold standard for wind and hail damage assessment,' with instructions to compare contractors by 'HAAG certification' and to hire a 'HAAG-certified contractor' (also in the conclusion: 'work with a locally established, HAAG-certified contractor'). NQR holds no such certification and the claim is fabricated.
defabToKill.fix: KILL all HAAG references. Reframe the selection criterion to documentation rigor: a test-square method, per-square impact counts, close-up photos with measurement references, and a roof diagram — plus verifiable active NJ HIC registration (13VH on the contract per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144) and a Certificate of Insurance. Insurers recognize well-documented, independent assessment (III; IBHS). NQR makes NO inspector-certification self-claim.

defabToKill.issue: Unsourced/invented dollar figures and stats: isolated repair '$400 to $1,500'; '$10,000 to $20,000 or more' replacement; deductible '$1,000 to $2,500'; wind/hail deductible '1 to 2 percent ... $2,000 to $5,000 on a $250,000 policy'; and the density threshold 'more than 8 to 10 impacts per test square.' None carry a named source.
defabToKill.fix: Use ONLY the gold's sourced cost tiers (each WITH attribution): minor $500–$1,500 (HomeAdvisor/Angi), moderate $1,500–$3,500 (This Old House/Angi), severe/partial-reroof $4,000–$12,000 (HomeAdvisor/Angi), few shingles from ~$150, one square $500–$1,500 (HomeAdvisor). Drop the invented deductible/threshold numbers; cite the III $14,747 average wind-and-hail claim as context. End with a free written estimate.

defabToKill.issue: Invented claim-window stats: 'Most NJ homeowner insurance policies require claims to be filed within one year of the damage event' and 'hail damage that goes undetected for 18 months may exceed your claim filing window.' No source; specific filing-deadline figures are fabricated.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the specific one-year / 18-month figures. State the grounded rationale instead: prompt inspection after a hailstorm documents impacts before later weather alters the evidence, which supports attributing damage to a specific storm for a claim (NRCA inspection cadence; III claim-documentation rationale). Do not invent a numeric filing deadline.

defabToKill.issue: Geographic/material embellishments stated as fact: 'standing seam metal roofs (increasingly common in parts of Montclair and Millburn),' wood shake and slate 'particularly vulnerable to hail in Essex County.' Unsupported local-prevalence and vulnerability claims.
defabToKill.fix: Keep the grounded signs only (bruises/soft spots, granule loss, cracked/split edges, dented metal, AC/vehicle collateral dents, neighbor claims — all per IBHS/AMS). If other materials are mentioned, do so generically without inventing local prevalence; ground metal denting as a corroborating indicator of hail size (IBHS), not a city-specific roof-type claim.

defabToKill.issue: Soft 'hundreds-style' authority phrasing 'the same methodology insurance adjusters use in Essex County' presented as a local proof point rather than a sourced fact.
defabToKill.fix: Attribute the test-square method to IBHS hail-assessment guidance as the standard inspection procedure adjusters and engineers use; do not localize it as an unsourced Essex-County-specific practice.

defabToKill.issue: First-person advocacy/scope claims implying special process: 'We routinely handle supplemental documentation' (in cost-guide) and decision-article framing that positions NQR as an insurance advocate. Risks implying licensed adjusting/public-adjuster activity.
defabToKill.fix: Frame NQR's role accurately: a registered NJ HIC documents the damage with test-square findings and meets the adjuster on-site to walk the documentation. Do NOT promise to 'handle' the claim, waive a deductible, or act as the homeowner's adjuster (a registered HIC is not a public adjuster). Keep the honest anti-fraud guidance (never sign before knowing coverage; refuse inflated-damage pressure).

defabToKill.issue: Watch for any residual de-fab the new copy must NOT introduce: GAF Master Elite / CertainTeed SELECT ShingleMaster / Owens Corning Preferred self-claims, 'only ~2% qualify,' Golden Pledge specifics, '24/7,' 'fully licensed/certified,' 'licensed NJ contractor,' 'hundreds of completed repairs/replacements,' or any invented dollar statistic.
defabToKill.fix: Make NO manufacturer-certification self-claim, NO '24/7' (gold hours are Mon–Fri 7:00 AM–6:00 PM, Sat 8:00 AM–2:00 PM), NO 'licensed' (use 'registered NJ HIC'), NO completed-job counts, and no dollar figure without a named source from the costRanges above.

parentDebtToAvoid: Commercial brand line — the parent gold says 'Newark Quality Roofing installs and services Firestone, Carlisle, and Johns Manville membrane systems.' Do NOT reproduce manufacturer brand-name system lines (Firestone/Carlisle/Johns Manville membranes; GAF/CertainTeed/Owens Corning shingle systems) in the new articles. Describe membrane types generically (EPDM, TPO, modified bitumen) without brand endorsement.

Credential chip — the parent gold credentialsHighlight lists 'NJ HIC Licensed.' This is WRONG: the articles must say 'registered NJ HIC' / 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor.' NJ issues no roofing license; HIC is a registration. Never write 'licensed.'

Cost framing (SERVICE NOTE verification) — VERIFY before copying the '$3,000–$12,000 hail-damage repair, per Angi' figure. Real Angi/HomeAdvisor data shows minor hail repairs run a few hundred to a few thousand dollars; once hail damage is widespread it typically drives a FULL REPLACEMENT priced per square, not a 'repair.' The $3k–$12k band conflates repair with partial replacement. AUTHOR INSTRUCTION: present the honest tiered framing — minor hail repair $500–$1,500 and moderate $1,500–$3,500 are true repairs (HomeAdvisor/Angi/This Old House); the $4,000–$12,000 band is severe damage that punctures underlayment or requires partial reroofing, i.e. a partial REPLACEMENT priced per square, NOT a like-for-like repair. Do not present '$3,000–$12,000 repair' as a single flat repair range, and never quote it as a naked number without its source.

No whole-job total — hasRealWholeProjectTotal is FALSE. The gold prices by repair tier / per square / per shingle, not a single whole-job dollar total. The new cost-guide article must NOT invent a 'typical full hail repair costs $X' whole-job number; lead with the free-written-estimate framing plus the sourced tiers, and note widespread damage usually means insurance-covered replacement priced per square.

articleAngles.signs: Definitively answer that the signs of hail damage are functional roof-surface impacts confirmed at close range, not from the ground: circular bruises/soft spots (mat fracture under intact granules — the primary functional sign), random-pattern granule loss exposing the black mat, cracked/split shingle edges, and dented metal gutters/vent caps/flashing — corroborated by AC-fin/vehicle dents and neighbor claims (all per IBHS hail-assessment guidance / AMS). Anchor damage thresholds: NOAA severe-hail warning at 0.75 in, but roof damage begins ~1.0 in (aged 3-tab) / ~1.25 in (most shingles), 2.0 in damages all roofing (AMS); kinetic energy = size + wind speed (IBHS). Prompt post-storm inspection documents impacts before weather alters evidence (NRCA cadence; III). DROP the one-year/18-month filing-window stat and Montclair/Millburn standing-seam embellishment.
articleAngles.costGuide: Definitively answer that hail repair has no single whole-job price — cost runs by tier and is often insurance-covered, so NQR gives a free written estimate and documents the damage for the claim. Cite ONLY sourced tiers: minor $500–$1,500 (HomeAdvisor/Angi), moderate $1,500–$3,500 (This Old House/Angi), severe/partial-reroof $4,000–$12,000 (HomeAdvisor/Angi); few shingles from ~$150 and one square $500–$1,500 (HomeAdvisor); Class 4 upgrade +10–20% with 10–35% premium discounts (RoofVista/TX DOI). Be honest that the upper band is partial REPLACEMENT priced per square, not a repair, and that widespread hail damage usually means a full replacement. Context: wind+hail are the largest homeowners claim type, average $14,747 (III, 2019–2023). STRIP the invented deductible/percentage/impact-threshold numbers.
articleAngles.decision: Definitively answer that you choose a hail-damage contractor by VERIFIABLE credentials and documentation rigor, NOT inspector certifications: active NJ HIC registration (13VH number on the contract per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144 — a registration, NOT a license), a Certificate of Insurance for ≥$500,000/occurrence general liability (N.J.S.A. 56:8-142) issued by the carrier, a written contract for work over $500 (N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2), an itemized written estimate, local references/established Essex County presence, and a thorough documented test-square assessment (per-square impact counts, photos with measurement references, roof diagram — the rigor insurers recognize, per IBHS and III). KILL HAAG entirely; replace 'hire a HAAG-certified contractor' with this verifiable-documentation standard. Keep honest anti-fraud guidance (no inflated-damage claims, no deductible waivers, never sign before knowing coverage). NQR's role = registered NJ HIC who documents and walks the adjuster through findings — NOT a public adjuster handling the claim.
